title: Cat Budgets: Reinsurers Used Far Less Than Primary Insurers in 2026
summary: A PolicyRix Team analysis of six European insurers and reinsurers finds the reinsurers had used roughly 40% to 74% of their 2026 catastrophe budgets by September, while AXA and Allianz, which carry more European hail and storm risk directly, took the heavier hit.
description:
Every big insurer sets aside a budget for natural catastrophes before the year starts, and the third-quarter reports published since late October show something useful when those budgets are placed side by side. The reinsurers, the companies that insure insurers, mostly finished September well inside what they had planned for. The primary insurers that sell home and business cover directly in Europe had a much rougher summer, because the costliest events of 2026 were hailstorms and storms that land mainly on their own books.

This PolicyRix Team analysis compares six groups: Swiss Re, Hannover Re, Munich Re, SCOR, AXA and Allianz. The figures come from each company's third-quarter or nine-month results, as covered in our earlier stories and in reporting on Swiss Re's release of November 5. The budget usage percentages are our own calculations. Each company defines its budget differently, so the comparison is a guide to direction, not a precise league table.

How much of the budget was used

Swiss Re's property and casualty reinsurance unit reported large natural catastrophe losses of 640 million US dollars for the first nine months against a full-year budget of 1.6 billion dollars, according to Insurance Business. On our calculation that is 40% of the annual budget used after three quarters of the year, or about 53% of a simple pro-rata nine-month budget of 1.2 billion dollars. The main events were the earthquake in Colombia in August and Storm Kristin in Portugal in January.

Hannover Re reported large losses, which include natural catastrophes and big man-made claims, of 1,316 million euros for nine months against a pro-rata budget of 1,786.5 million euros. That is about 74% of the nine-month budget on our calculation, leaving roughly 470 million euros unused, and about 57% of the full-year budget of 2.3 billion euros.

SCOR reported a nine-month natural catastrophe ratio of 5.4% against a budget of 10%. In budget terms that is 54% used. Its third quarter was heavier, at 9.1%, so the year-to-date figure hides a busier summer.

Munich Re gives its budget as a share of revenue rather than a money amount. Major losses in the third quarter were 14.9% of net insurance revenue against the 18% it expected, which is about 83% of the quarterly budget on our calculation. The Colombian El Choco earthquake was the costliest single event at 300 million euros.

The primary insurers look different. AXA said natural catastrophe losses exceeded its prorated annual budget of 4.5 points of combined ratio, driven by secondary perils, mainly hail and storms in France, Switzerland and Italy. Allianz did not give a budget comparison in the figures we used, but natural catastrophes added 5.1 points to its third-quarter property and casualty combined ratio, against 0.3 points a year earlier, and Beinsure put the quarter's catastrophe claims at about 1.07 billion euros, most of it from European storms, hail and wildfires.

Why reinsurers were spared

Our reading, which is an interpretation rather than something the companies stated, is that the pattern reflects who carries which layer of risk. A hailstorm causes thousands of medium-sized claims across cars, roofs and windows. Each claim is small, and the insurer that sold the policy usually pays most of the total itself, because its reinsurance only starts paying once losses from one event pass a high threshold. Earthquakes and very large windstorms are the events that reach deep into reinsurance programmes. In 2026, the big European losses were the frequent, medium-sized kind, and the large single events were limited, so the burden fell on primary insurers.

There is a second reason. Reinsurers spent the past few years raising prices and the point at which their cover starts. Swiss Re's own figures show the effect of softer pricing now: its P&C reinsurance revenue fell 8.6% to 12.8 billion dollars for nine months, and its July renewals cleared at a net price decrease of 5.3%, according to a summary of its presentation. Even so, its nine-month P&C combined ratio was 77.3%, a very wide margin.

What it means for policyholders

For homeowners and drivers, the reinsurance numbers are an early signal rather than a bill. When reinsurers have a light year and their prices are falling, the cost of protection that home insurers buy usually eases at the next renewal, which for many European and global programmes is January 1, 2027. That can take some pressure off home premiums over time. Against that, the insurers that sell to households, such as AXA and Allianz, are paying more of the hail and storm claims themselves, and those costs tend to show up in pricing for the regions hit hardest. A household in an area that had repeated hail claims should not assume cheaper reinsurance will translate into a lower renewal quote.

What the data cannot tell us

The fourth quarter is not in these numbers, and it includes the end of the Atlantic hurricane season and European winter storms. Budgets are defined differently: Swiss Re counts large natural catastrophes, Hannover Re includes man-made losses, SCOR uses a ratio and Munich Re a quarterly share of revenue. The figures also span three currencies. Finally, budget usage says nothing about whether a company's prices are adequate for next year, which is what ultimately decides what policyholders pay.

The short version is that 2026 has so far been a year of many medium-sized weather losses rather than one huge event, and that shape of year rewards reinsurers and penalises the companies that sell cover directly to households.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of nine-month and third-quarter 2026 results from Swiss Re, Hannover Re, Munich Re, SCOR, AXA and Allianz, using Insurance Business, Reinsurance News and earlier PolicyRix coverage
image_alt: A tornado under dark storm clouds over a green field (illustrative)
key_points: Swiss Re's P&C reinsurance unit used about 40% of its 1.6 billion dollar full-year natural catastrophe budget in nine months, with losses of 640 million dollars, on our calculation.
Hannover Re's large losses of 1,316 million euros were about 74% of its nine-month budget, leaving roughly 470 million euros unused, and SCOR's 5.4% catastrophe ratio was 54% of its 10% budget.
Munich Re's third-quarter major losses were 14.9% of revenue against 18% expected, about 83% of the quarterly budget, with the El Choco earthquake its costliest event.
AXA said hail and storm losses breached its prorated 4.5-point budget, and catastrophes added 5.1 points to Allianz's third-quarter combined ratio against 0.3 points a year earlier.
Our interpretation is that frequent, medium-sized hail and storm losses stayed with primary insurers, while softer reinsurance pricing may ease costs at January 2027 renewals.
why_it_matters: Catastrophe budgets show where the year's weather costs actually landed. If reinsurers had a light year and prices are falling, home insurers' protection costs may ease, but the insurers selling to households absorbed the hail and storm claims themselves, which can keep premiums high in the regions hit hardest.

title: UK Mortgages: The Math of a 5.97% Fix Versus a 4.68% Tracker
summary: With the average two-year fix at 5.97% and the average two-year tracker at 4.68%, a PolicyRix Team calculation shows a tracker borrower would need Bank Rate to rise about 1.3 points almost at once to pay as much as a fixer over two years.
description:
UK borrowers coming off fixed deals this winter face a choice that looks unusual. After the Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% on November 5, the average two-year fixed mortgage rate stood at 5.97% at the start of November while the average two-year tracker, which moves with Bank Rate, was 4.68%, according to Moneyfacts. Normally a borrower pays a premium for a tracker's uncertainty. Right now the tracker is the cheaper product by more than a full percentage point, and the obvious question is what has to happen for that gap to close.

This PolicyRix Team analysis works through the numbers on an example loan. The rates are Moneyfacts averages reported by Moneyfacts and by the trade publication Mortgage Professional (MPA); the repayment figures are our own calculations using a standard repayment formula. They ignore arrangement fees, which vary widely and can change the answer for a smaller loan.

How fixed rates got here

The Moneyfacts average two-year fixed rate rose from 4.83% in January to 5.97% at the start of November, its highest since December 2023, and the five-year average reached 6.00%. The Moneyfacts Average New Mortgage Rate climbed to 5.89%, a three-year high. Lenders price fixed deals off swap rates, which reflect where markets expect interest rates to go, and Moneyfacts linked much of the rise to swap volatility and to lenders repricing ahead of the rate rise. In other words, fixed rates already include an expectation that Bank Rate will go higher.

The example: 200,000 pounds over 25 years

On our calculation, a 200,000 pound repayment mortgage over 25 years costs:

At 4.83%, January's average two-year fix: about 1,149 pounds a month.
At 5.97%, November's average two-year fix: about 1,285 pounds a month.
At 4.68%, November's average two-year tracker: about 1,132 pounds a month.

So a borrower who could have fixed in January and is fixing now pays roughly 135 pounds a month more, or about 1,626 pounds a year, for the same loan. And today's fixer pays about 153 pounds a month more than today's tracker borrower, which adds up to about 3,666 pounds over a two-year deal if the tracker rate never moved.

What would close the gap

We calculated the tracker rate at which the monthly payment matches the 5.97% fix. It is 5.97% itself, which means Bank Rate would need to rise by about 1.29 percentage points straight away and stay there for two years before the tracker cost the same as fixing. A slower path leaves the tracker ahead. In a scenario where Bank Rate rises another 0.25 points after six months and a further 0.25 points after a year, our two-year tracker total is about 28,042 pounds against 30,839 pounds for the fix, a saving of roughly 2,796 pounds. That scenario is an illustration, not a forecast.

For context on sensitivity, our formula puts each 0.25 point move at about 36 pounds a month on a 250,000 pound, 25-year loan, close to the 37 pounds Moneyfacts estimated for the November rise. On the 200,000 pound example, each quarter point is about 29 pounds a month.

What the Bank has said

The Bank of England's November decision was an 8-1 vote, with one member preferring a half-point rise. Governor Andrew Bailey said the increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes, while the Bank projected inflation at about 5% by mid-2027. The next decision is due on December 17. Those statements cut both ways for a tracker borrower: the Bank is not promising a run of rises, but inflation is expected to climb before it falls.

What it means for borrowers

A tracker is cheaper today and would stay cheaper unless rates rise sharply and quickly. The trade-off is certainty. A fixed payment makes budgeting simple and protects a household that could not absorb a jump of a few hundred pounds a month if inflation surprised badly. Borrowers weighing a tracker should check whether the deal has early repayment charges, because some trackers allow switching to a fix later without penalty, which gives a way out if rates start rising faster than expected. Those with little headroom in their budgets may reasonably decide that paying for certainty is worth it.

What the data cannot tell us

Averages hide a wide spread: the best deals at low loan-to-value ratios are well below 5.97%, and borrowers with small deposits pay more. Fees are excluded and can add more than a thousand pounds. Our scenarios assume rate changes pass straight through to trackers, which is how most work, but terms differ. Nobody knows the path of Bank Rate, and markets can move swap rates and fixed pricing within days.

The arithmetic is clear on one point: at today's averages, the fixed-rate premium is large enough that it pays for a lot of future rate rises before a tracker loses out.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis using Moneyfacts average mortgage rates (via Moneyfactscompare.co.uk and Mortgage Professional) and the Bank of England's November 5, 2026 decision
image_alt: Suburban house with a front lawn (illustrative)
key_points: Moneyfacts put the average two-year fix at 5.97% at the start of November, up from 4.83% in January, while the average two-year tracker was 4.68%.
On our calculation a 200,000 pound, 25-year loan costs about 1,285 pounds a month at 5.97%, 1,149 pounds at 4.83% and 1,132 pounds at 4.68%.
A tracker borrower would need Bank Rate to rise about 1.29 points almost at once, and stay there, to pay as much as a fixer over two years.
In an illustrative path of two further quarter-point rises, the tracker still saves about 2,796 pounds over two years before fees.
The fix buys certainty; the figures exclude fees, and averages hide a wide spread by deposit size.
why_it_matters: Hundreds of thousands of UK borrowers must choose a new deal as fixes end. Knowing how far rates would need to rise before a tracker costs more than a fix turns a gut decision into a number a household can test against its own budget.

title: Medicare 2027: Which Costs Are Final and Which Are Still Estimates
summary: With Medicare open enrollment ending December 7, a PolicyRix Team breakdown shows the Part D cap rises to $2,400 and the deductible to $700 for 2027, while the $209.50 Part B premium is still a Trustees projection, and a high drug user could pay about $416 more in total.
description:
Medicare open enrollment runs until December 7, and people choosing a plan for 2027 are working with a mix of firm numbers and estimates. Some 2027 costs were finalised months ago. Others, including the standard Part B premium that most beneficiaries pay, had not been published by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services in the sources we checked when this was written, and are still based on the projection in the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report. Knowing which is which matters, because plan choices are locked in for the year.

This PolicyRix Team explainer sets out what is final, what is projected, and what the changes add up to for an example beneficiary. The figures come from published CMS amounts and the Trustees Report as reported by several Medicare information sites; the totals are our own calculations.

What is already final for 2027

The Part D prescription drug figures are set. The standard Part D deductible rises to $700 from $615, an increase of about 14%. The annual out-of-pocket cap on covered drug costs rises to $2,400 from $2,100, an increase of $300, or about 14%. CMS also set the national base beneficiary premium, a benchmark used in calculating Part D premiums and late enrollment penalties, at $41.33 a month, up about 6% from $38.99. The base premium is not what any particular plan charges; each plan sets its own premium.

What is still a projection

The 2026 Trustees Report estimated the 2027 standard Part B premium at $209.50 a month, up $6.60, or about 3.3%, from $202.90 in 2026. It projected the Part B deductible at $292, up $9 from $283. The Part A hospital deductible and the income brackets for higher-income surcharges, known as IRMAA, are also announced with the Part B premium. CMS released the 2026 figures on November 14, 2025, and the 2025 figures on November 8, 2024, so the official 2027 numbers are due around now. Some private forecasts have suggested a higher premium, so the Trustees figure is a reasonable planning number rather than a certainty.

Separately, the administration announced in October a one-time $90 payment to about 20.8 million original Medicare beneficiaries to help with Part B premiums, according to AARP. On the projected 2027 premium, $90 would cover about 43% of one month.

Worked example: a beneficiary with high drug costs

Consider someone in original Medicare with a stand-alone Part D plan whose drug costs are high enough to reach the out-of-pocket cap. Using the national base premium as a stand-in for the plan premium, which is a simplification, our calculation of the main annual costs is:

2026: Part B premium of $2,434.80, Part B deductible of $283, Part D cap of $2,100 and base Part D premium of $467.88, a total of about $5,286.

2027: Part B premium of $2,514 at the projected rate, Part B deductible of $292, Part D cap of $2,400 and base Part D premium of $495.96, a total of about $5,702.

That is an increase of about $416, or roughly 8%, and most of it comes from the higher drug cap. For someone with low drug costs who never reaches the Part D deductible, the change is much smaller and comes mainly from the Part B premium, which on the projection rises by about $79 for the year.

What it means for people choosing a plan

The rise in the drug cap is the change most likely to affect heavy medication users, and it is already certain. People who expect to hit the cap should compare plans on total yearly cost, using Medicare's plan finder with their actual drug list, rather than on monthly premium alone. A plan with a higher premium can be cheaper overall if it covers a key drug at a lower tier. People with Medicare Advantage should check whether their plan's drug coverage, network or extra benefits changed for 2027, since plans can change each year. Anyone whose income was high in 2025 should watch for the IRMAA brackets, because the 2027 surcharge is based on the 2025 tax return.

What the data cannot tell us

The Part B premium and deductible in our example are projections and may change when CMS publishes the official amounts. Actual Part D premiums vary by plan and region, and many beneficiaries receive help through Extra Help or employer coverage. The example ignores Part B coinsurance, which is 20% of approved costs after the deductible and can be large, as well as supplemental Medigap premiums. Social Security cost-of-living adjustments also offset part of the increase for many people.

The firm takeaway is that drug costs at the top end are going up by $300 next year regardless of the Part B announcement, and open enrollment is the window to choose a plan with that in mind.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of 2027 Medicare amounts published by CMS and projected in the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report, as reported by AARP, Kiplinger, BenefitsUSA and other Medicare information sites
image_alt: Doctor speaking with an older patient representing Medicare coverage decisions (illustrative)
key_points: Final for 2027: the Part D deductible rises to $700 from $615 and the out-of-pocket drug cap to $2,400 from $2,100, while the national base beneficiary premium is $41.33.
Still projected: the Trustees Report puts the standard Part B premium at $209.50 a month, up $6.60, and the Part B deductible at $292.
CMS published 2026 amounts on November 14, 2025, so the official 2027 Part B figures are due around now.
On our example, a beneficiary who hits the drug cap faces about $5,702 of main costs in 2027 against about $5,286 in 2026, an increase of about $416.
Open enrollment ends December 7; heavy drug users should compare total yearly cost, not premium alone.
why_it_matters: Medicare plan choices are locked in for a year, and open enrollment closes on December 7. Separating confirmed 2027 costs from estimates helps beneficiaries budget correctly and pick a plan on total cost, especially those with high drug bills facing a $300 higher cap.

title: Co-operators Swings to Q3 Underwriting Loss as Prairie Storms Hit
summary: Co-operators General posted a third-quarter underwriting loss of $139.9 million and a combined ratio of 109.7%, against 90.0% a year earlier, as Canada's third-costliest summer for insured weather losses and weaker bond results hit the insurer.
description:
Co-operators General Insurance Company, one of Canada's largest home and auto insurers, swung to an underwriting loss in the third quarter of 2026 as severe summer weather drove up claims. The company reported an underwriting loss of $139.9 million, excluding discounting and risk adjustment, against underwriting income of $141.4 million a year earlier, a deterioration of $281.3 million. Its combined ratio rose to 109.7% from 90.0%, a 19.7 point swing. Figures are in Canadian dollars.

The results were released on November 9. This article is based on the company's news release and reporting by Insurance Business Canada.

What changed

A combined ratio compares claims and expenses with premiums, so a figure above 100% means the insurer paid out more than it earned from underwriting in the quarter. Co-operators' chief executive, Rob Wesseling, said the quarter reflected a challenging period, with significant weather events and higher claims activity putting pressure on underwriting, alongside lower investment results. Insurance Business reported that the company did not disclose its own catastrophe loss figure.

The wider backdrop was a costly summer. Citing the Insurance Bureau of Canada and CatIQ, Insurance Business reported that ten extreme weather events across Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba caused more than $1.8 billion of insured damage, and that national insured losses for the summer topped $3.7 billion, the third-costliest summer on record.

For the first nine months, the combined ratio was 99.6%, against 95.5% a year earlier. On our reading, that means the strong first half was almost entirely used up by the third quarter. Year-to-date net income was $279.5 million, down from $450.6 million, a fall of about 38% on our calculation.

Premiums and investments

Direct written premiums, the value of policies written before reinsurance, rose 1.9% to $1,631.6 million in the quarter. Home premiums grew 5.4% and auto 0.7%, while commercial premiums declined. Net insurance revenue rose 2.8% to $1,450.8 million.

Investments did not help this time. Net investment income and gains were $22.9 million, down $158.8 million from the same quarter of 2025, mainly because of losses on the bond portfolio compared with gains a year earlier.

Capital remains above requirements

The company's Minimum Capital Test ratio, the main Canadian measure of an insurer's capital strength, was 219% at September 30, down from 224% at the end of 2025 and well above internal and regulatory minimums. Shareholders' equity rose to $3,088.4 million from $3,019.4 million, and the company paid $189.1 million of dividends in the first nine months. Wesseling said the capital position remained strong.

How it compares

The result fits a pattern across Canadian property insurers this quarter. Intact reported a group combined ratio of 94.0% with about C$660 million of catastrophe losses, and its Canadian personal property line ran at 105.0%. Definity reported 100.6%, with catastrophes adding 12.8 points. Co-operators' 109.7% is the highest of the three, which is consistent with its larger share of home insurance in the Prairies, although the company's release does not break that down.

What it means for policyholders

For Co-operators customers, the immediate message is that the insurer has the capital to pay claims, with a capital ratio more than double the usual supervisory target. The longer-term question is price. When an insurer's home book loses money in a heavy weather year, rate increases at renewal usually follow in the regions most affected. Homeowners in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba should expect renewal quotes to reflect this summer's losses, and it is worth reviewing deductibles, sewer backup and overland water coverage, and whether hail-resistant roofing could qualify for a discount.

Two terms worth knowing

Co-operators reports its combined ratio excluding discounting and risk adjustment. Under the IFRS 17 accounting standard, insurers can discount future claim payments to today's value and add a margin for uncertainty, and both adjustments move the ratio. Stripping them out, as Co-operators does in this measure, gives a figure closer to the plain comparison of claims and expenses against premiums that most readers expect. The Minimum Capital Test, set by Canada's federal regulator, compares the capital an insurer holds with the capital needed for the risks it carries; supervisors generally expect insurers to stay above 150%, so a reading of 219% leaves a wide cushion even after a loss-making quarter.

For comparison, Co-operators had a far better third quarter in 2025, when its combined ratio of 90.0% was a 24.7 point improvement on the storm-hit third quarter of 2024. The swing from one year to the next shows how much a single summer of weather can move a home-heavy insurer's results.

What we do not know

The company did not publish its catastrophe loss amount for the quarter or split losses by province, so we cannot say how much of the deterioration came from any single event. The fourth quarter will show whether claims from the summer events continue to develop.

The next update will come with full-year results in February.
source_name: Co-operators General Insurance Company third-quarter 2026 results (CNW release, November 9, 2026) and Insurance Business Canada
image_alt: Flooded residential street after heavy rain (illustrative)
key_points: Co-operators General's third-quarter underwriting loss was $139.9 million against income of $141.4 million a year earlier, and the combined ratio rose to 109.7% from 90.0%.
Insurance Business, citing IBC and CatIQ, reported more than $1.8 billion of insured Prairie storm damage and over $3.7 billion nationally, the third-costliest summer on record.
Nine-month combined ratio was 99.6% against 95.5%, and year-to-date net income fell to $279.5 million from $450.6 million.
Premiums rose 1.9% to $1,631.6 million, but net investment income and gains fell $158.8 million to $22.9 million on bond losses.
The Minimum Capital Test ratio was 219%, down from 224% but well above requirements.
why_it_matters: Co-operators insures a large share of Canadian homes, especially in the Prairies. A loss-making quarter driven by weather usually feeds into home insurance rates at renewal, so policyholders in the hardest-hit provinces should review cover and expect pricing to reflect the summer's storms.

title: ACCC Says IAG's RAC Insurance Deal Unlikely to Benefit the Public
summary: The ACCC has told IAG its bid for RAC Insurance in Western Australia is unlikely to deliver a net public benefit, rejecting a package of undertakings; IAG must respond by December 1 and a final decision is due on February 1, 2027.
description:
Australia's competition regulator has given an early thumbs-down to Insurance Australia Group's latest attempt to buy RAC Insurance, the market-leading car and home insurer in Western Australia. In a public benefit assessment summary published on November 10, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission said there is unlikely to be a net public benefit from the acquisition, because the benefits are likely to be outweighed by the harm to competition. IAG must respond by December 1, and a final determination is due on February 1, 2027.

This article is based on reporting by Insurance Business Australia and on the ACCC's earlier media releases on the deal.

How the deal got here

IAG, which sells insurance under the NRMA brand in Western Australia, first sought clearance in 2025 under the old informal merger system, and the ACCC opposed it in December 2025. At that time the ACCC said the combined business would have roughly 55% to 65% of motor insurance and 50% to 60% of home and contents insurance in the state. IAG then notified the deal under Australia's new formal merger regime, which began on January 1, 2026, and the ACCC again decided in September 2026 that it must not proceed. In October, IAG lodged a public benefit application, which asks the regulator to approve a deal that harms competition if the wider benefits are larger. IAG and RAC also applied to the Australian Competition Tribunal for a merits review, which is on hold while the application is considered.

Under the proposal, IAG would buy all of RAC Insurance, and RAC would keep selling RAC-branded insurance in Western Australia for 20 years under an exclusive distribution and brand licensing agreement.

What IAG offered

To win approval, IAG offered a ten-year court-enforceable undertaking. It included selling the renewal rights to its active NRMA home and motor book in Western Australia, commitments on access and conduct for smash repairers, keeping a contact centre in the state, extending RAC-branded home and contents cover to eligible homes north of the 26th parallel, a dedicated community fund and an optional transfer of the SGIO brand.

Why the ACCC was not persuaded

The ACCC accepted that some public benefits were likely, but said the parties had overstated their size and underestimated how long they would take. It said cost savings estimates did not properly compare the position with and without the deal and may not include integration costs. It did not consider a larger reinsurance programme or community investment to be significant benefits, noting that RAC would likely fund community activities anyway. On the undertaking, it cited material execution risk, uncertain customer retention and inadequate protections for the sale of NRMA renewal rights, and said the smash repair commitments would not replicate the competition between two independent buyers of repairs. It also said expansion north of the 26th parallel would add no competition because IAG already operates there.

Central to the view was what happens without the deal. The ACCC said that in the absence of the acquisition, RAC Insurance would remain an independent competitor to IAG.

IAG said it remains confident the alliance would deliver long-term benefits for members, customers and communities, disagreed with the preliminary view and said it would keep engaging with the regulator.

What it means for policyholders

For drivers and homeowners in Western Australia, the regulator's concern is about choice and price. The ACCC's earlier finding was that rival insurers have historically struggled to grow in the state, so combining the two largest players could reduce the pressure that keeps premiums and claims service competitive. Nothing changes for existing RAC or NRMA policies while the process runs. If the deal is ultimately blocked, RAC Insurance continues as a stand-alone insurer; if it were approved, policies would still carry the RAC brand, but the underwriter would be IAG.

The wider pattern

The deal is part of a run of tie-ups between Australian insurers and member-owned motoring clubs. IAG completed its 855 million dollar purchase of RACQ Insurance in Queensland in September 2025 under a 25-year exclusive distribution agreement, and Allianz bought RAA's general insurance business in South Australia for 642 million dollars in July 2025 under a 20-year arrangement, according to Insurance Business. If the RAC deal went ahead, RACT in Tasmania would be the only motoring club in the country still running its own general insurance business. Insurance Business has put the RAC transaction at 1.35 billion Australian dollars, although the latest report did not restate the value.

The Motor Trades Association of Australia, which represents repairers, has opposed the deal and earlier rejected IAG's proposed behavioural undertaking, arguing it would entrench insurer concentration in the state's motor repair market.

What comes next

IAG's response is due by December 1, and the ACCC's final determination is scheduled for February 1, 2027. The Tribunal review remains available. The case is one of the first major insurance tests of the new merger regime, and the outcome will be watched by other member-owned motoring clubs and insurers considering similar distribution deals.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia (November 11, 2026) and ACCC media releases on IAG's proposed acquisition of RAC Insurance
image_alt: Business handshake representing a proposed insurance acquisition (illustrative)
key_points: In a summary published November 10, the ACCC said there is unlikely to be a net public benefit from IAG's acquisition of RAC Insurance.
IAG must respond by December 1, and the final determination is due on February 1, 2027; a Tribunal merits review is on hold meanwhile.
IAG offered a ten-year undertaking including the sale of NRMA's WA home and motor renewal rights, smash repairer commitments and a community fund.
The ACCC cited execution risk and uncertain customer retention, and said RAC Insurance would otherwise remain an independent competitor.
In December 2025 the ACCC estimated the combined group would hold about 55% to 65% of WA motor and 50% to 60% of home and contents insurance.
why_it_matters: RAC Insurance and IAG are the two biggest car and home insurers in Western Australia. Whether they combine affects how much competition there is on premiums and claims service for millions of policies in the state.

title: Liberty Mutual Q3 Profit Falls 7% as Personal Lines Premiums Shrink
summary: Liberty Mutual's third-quarter net income fell 7% to $2.07 billion as catastrophe losses rose to $585 million and its combined ratio climbed to 89.5%, while $840 million of reserve releases cushioned weaker underlying results and US personal lines premiums fell 5.6%.
description:
Liberty Mutual, one of the largest US home and auto insurers, reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $2.07 billion, down 7% from $2.22 billion a year earlier. The combined ratio, which compares claims and expenses with premiums, rose 4.8 points to 89.5% from 84.7%, as catastrophe losses climbed to $585 million from $114 million. Over nine months, net income rose 32.6% to $6.75 billion and the combined ratio improved 1.4 points to 88.1%, helped by much lower catastrophe losses than in early 2025, when the Los Angeles wildfires struck.

The results were released on November 5. This article draws on reporting by Reinsurance News, Business Insurance, Insurance Business and Coverager, which agree on the main figures.

What changed

The headline numbers were held up by reserve releases. Favourable prior-year development, meaning claims from earlier years cost less than the company had set aside, was $840 million, more than double the $416 million a year earlier, and improved the combined ratio by 7.7 points, according to Insurance Business. Limited partnership income, from private equity and similar investments, rose 36% to $810 million.

Underneath, underwriting was weaker. The underlying combined ratio, which strips out catastrophes and prior-year development, rose 4.5 points to 91.9% from 87.4%. Most of that came from expenses: the underwriting expense ratio rose to 35.4% from 31.4%. Insurance Business noted that the release did not explain the increase. Catastrophes added 5.3 points to the combined ratio, against 1.0 point a year earlier.

Premiums shrinking in personal lines

Total net written premiums fell 2.8% to $10.74 billion. US Retail Markets, which sells personal auto and home insurance, wrote $6.72 billion, down 5.6%, and is down 2.8% over nine months. Global Risk Solutions, the commercial and specialty business, was broadly flat at $4.0 billion. Revenue rose 1.2% to $12.88 billion, and total equity reached $44.37 billion, up 11.2% from the end of 2025.

The company also agreed to buy Brazilian surety provider Austral Seguradora, with closing expected in 2027 subject to approvals.

Chief executive Tim Sweeney described the period as another excellent quarter, pointing to the $2.1 billion of net income and the 89.5% combined ratio.

What it means for policyholders

For drivers and homeowners, the more telling numbers are below the headline. A shrinking personal lines book alongside a sharp rise in expenses often signals that an insurer is spending more on advertising, commissions or technology to win customers in a market that has turned more competitive. Insurance Business noted that personal auto premiums across the industry are forecast to dip slightly in 2026 after several years of steep rate increases, and that some carriers have begun filing rate decreases in certain states.

For consumers, that combination is usually good news at renewal time. When large insurers compete for customers, shopping around is more likely to produce a lower quote, especially for auto cover. Policyholders whose premiums rose sharply in 2023 and 2024 may find that comparing quotes now is worth the effort. Home insurance is a different story in catastrophe-exposed states, where pricing still depends heavily on local weather losses.

How this fits the past year

The shrinking personal lines book is not new. Liberty Mutual's US Retail Markets premiums fell in every quarter of 2025, by between about 5% and 7%, with private passenger auto taking most of the decline, as the company focused on restoring profit after the losses of 2022 and 2023. That strategy worked: full-year 2025 net income rose 55% to about 6.8 billion dollars and the combined ratio improved 7.5 points to 88.4%, ahead of a 95% target the company set three years earlier. Executives said in March that they would pursue disciplined, targeted growth where they see a clear advantage. The third quarter shows the next phase: margins are still healthy, but they are being supported more by reserve releases and investment income, and the company is spending more while its personal lines premiums keep falling.

What the data cannot tell us

Reserve releases are a one-off support for profit and cannot be counted on every quarter, so the underlying ratio of 91.9% is a better guide to current pricing and claims costs than the headline figure. The release does not say why expenses rose, or how premium changes break down between auto and home. Liberty Mutual is a mutual holding company owned by its policyholders rather than listed shareholders, so its disclosures are less detailed than those of listed peers.

The fourth-quarter and full-year results are due in early 2027.
